svg.aria-label: Wireframe chapter 5 (desktop 1280px): In 2011 First Nations Australians were hospitalised after road crashes at about the same rate as everyone else. By 2021 the rate was half as high again.
svg.title: Wireframe chapter 5 (desktop 1280px): In 2011 First Nations Australians were hospitalised after road crashes at about the same rate as everyone else. By 2021 the rate was half as high again.

g.text: crashes at about the same rate as
Counts alone hide this, because the population grew. Per person,
the picture changes. Part of the rise may be better recording of
Indigenous status in hospital records, and these records cannot say
First Nations hospitalisations rose from 1,167 in 2011 to 2,220 in 2021 (+90%). For
Per 100,000 people, First Nations rose from about 145 to 226 (+56%); non-Indigenous
Part of the rise may be better recording of Indigenous status. Records with status
First Nations hospitalisations nearly doubled; everyone else's rose
Notes: Per 100,000 = hospitalisations / population x 100,000. Population figures are ABS estimates, back-cast after the 2021 Census (CC BY 4.0). Hospital records
Pedestrians are a bigger share of First Nations road-crash
Notes: Shares of each group's hospitalisations, pooled 2016-2021; not rates, and no data on how much each group walks, rides or drives. BITRE suppresses small
In remote areas, First Nations people are 41% of those hospitalised
Notes: Remoteness is where people usually live, not where the crash happened. We have no population by remoteness in this data, so we can't say whether 41% is high
This chapter describes hospital records. It is not about blame or choices, and it cannot say
why rates differ. It cannot tell us how much of the rise is better recording, how much each
group travels by foot, bike or car, or where the crashes happened.
